Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I should have protected others and I failed

vignette: Three years ago, David’s transit bus broke down in a condemned warehouse district after midnight. What was supposed to be a short wait for a tow became a prolonged detention. Armed men forced him off the vehicle and into a cold concrete room, where they questioned him, struck him, and bound his wrists while his passengers waited helplessly in the darkened bus outside. He watched a young mother clutch her child through the dirty glass, unable to reach her, unable to shield anyone from the violence unfolding behind him. When officers finally breached the room, David staggered out, but the image of his own helplessness remained. In the months that followed, David found himself bracing before he could even piece together the sequence of events. Certain nights in that warehouse were etched in his mind with terrifying precision—the metallic scrape of a chair leg, the smell of damp concrete, the sharp sting of a blow against his jaw. Other stretches of those fourteen hours slipped away entirely, leaving him with only fragments, as though a heavy fog had swallowed the rest. Whenever those sharp fragments surfaced, the terror rose in him exactly as it had then, a sudden, suffocating wave that made his breath catch and his palms sweat. He would sit in his kitchen, gripping the counter, certain that his mind was fracturing because he could not hold onto the whole story at once. Alongside these memories, his home environment grew tense. He had come to believe that safety was no longer a given, especially after dusk. While the daylight hours felt manageable, the dark hours brought a sharp, watchful dread. He would lie awake, straining his ears against the house’s settling noises, listening intently for the creak of a floorboard or the turn of a lock that might mean someone was entering. When the wind rattled the siding or a stray dog bumped against the fence, his heart would hammer against his ribs, his muscles locking tight as if bracing for another blow. He told himself it was simply a matter of staying watchful, but the physical reactions came too fast, too fierce, to be ignored. David’s work as a bus driver became a daily test of endurance. The depot parking lot, usually just a stretch of cracked asphalt and diesel fumes, now felt like a place that demanded constant readiness. When a passenger slammed the fare door behind him or the engine caught in a sudden backfire on a nearby street, his body would jolt, his breath hitching before he could steady himself. He began taking a different route to the terminal, arriving forty minutes early to park far from the driver’s lounge, avoiding the tight corridors where the air felt too close. His wife, Claire, noticed the distance creeping between them. He stopped answering evening calls, finding himself stepping away when the phone rang, unable to predict what the voice on the other end might say, and the quiet tension at the dinner table grew heavier each week. What kept David awake was not just the fear, but the quiet certainty that he had failed in the one way that mattered. He replayed the warehouse room, convinced he was a weak person who could not endure or defend. He would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened, for standing there while others suffered, for letting the chain of events unfold without resistance. He was certain that any man with a spine would have fought back or shielded his passengers, and his inability to do so settled into a heavy, unshakable weight in his chest. When Claire finally sat him down, laying out his sleeplessness, the way he flinched at sudden noises, and the way he had begun to isolate himself from the crew, David agreed to see a clinician. He did not expect a miracle, but he hoped someone might help him untangle the terror so he could finally rest through the night and look his passengers in the eye without bracing for the next attack.
